To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) age discrimination in personnel selection decisions is a function of the age-related information that is available to the selector at the time of decision-making and (2) the age bias effect is not generalizable between managers and students, or between high- and low-status jobs.
the age bias effect is moderated by the information condition and that managers are less susceptible to age bias than are students.
(1) age related information exposure affects managers' and students' selection decisions, and (2) the effect of age bias on selection decisions is not generalizable across samples.
In summary, our research is concerned with
age discrimination in selection decisions.
the effects of age related information on the age discrimination effect in personnel selection.
the effects of information exposure on selection decision making and the generalizability of selection research findings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of information, the applicant's age is a factor in the decision to hire.
age bias is an important issue in personnel selection and should not be dismissed.
age related information exposure affects the age discrimination in selection decisions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results indicate that information exposure does affect the age bias in selection decisions and that student subjects do not appear to generalize to managers in terms of their age bias effect.

age discrimination in selection decisions is not a function of the applicant's age per se, but is a result of information exposure that may be manipulated by the selection system to produce age discrimination.
, while the age bias effect is not a function of the information exposure variable, it is a function of the status of the job.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in a selection interview setting, age-related information can affect managers and student selectors differently.
the age discrimination in selection decisions can be eliminated by providing the selectors with information about the age of the applicants.
the age discrimination effect is not a stable phenomenon.
